newsitem.title: USA: U.N. official says U.S. did not get Iraq consensus.
newsitem.headline: U.N. official says U.S. did not get Iraq consensus.

text.p: The top U.N. peacekeeping official on Friday criticised the United States for failing to secure an international consensus for its missile strikes against Iraq last week.

Kofi Annan, Under-Secretary-General for Peacekeeping Operations, said U.N. members had the "feeling that there wasn't enough consultation before the U.S. acted." He told reporters, "We are seeing the fallout and the reactions."

U.S. forces fired cruise missiles at Iraqi defence installations after Baghdad's troops intervened on Aug. 30 in the Western-protected Kurdish region of northern Iraq. U.S. officials said they feared Iraq might move on to attack Kuwait or other countries to its south.

But few governments openly supported the U.S. strikes. A U.S.-backed British attempt to get a U.N. condemnation of Iraq's incursion into the north had to be abandoned last week after Russia threated a veto.

Annan noted that when Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, Western powers developed "a very formidable coalition" that eventually ejected Iraqi forces from Kuwait. "This time round it looks as if either consultations were not effective or had not been concluded before the attacks on Iraq began," he said.

Annan, a Ghanaian who has been mentioned as a possible future secretary-general, conceded U.S. leaders were under time pressure to prevent Iraq from further action. But he said "with Iraq it would also have been useful to try and keep a coalition together. Because that had not happened we have seen the divisions in the Security Council and elsewhere."
Despite assertions that the anti-Iraq coalition is intact, U.S. officials have shown signs of disappointment at the lukewarm support from allies in Europe and the Middle East.

Secretary of State Warren Christopher on Thursday called in ambassadors from the Gulf states, most of which have remained tight-lipped about the U.S. missile strikes, to underline the threat Washington believes they face from Iraq.

Former Central Intelligence Agency Director James Woolsey suggested on Friday Arab states would be more supportive if they thought Washington planned serious action against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein instead of pinprick missile strikes.

"You're going to get criticism of the United States ... as long as they don't think we're really serious," he said on ABC television. "I think if they think we're going to seriously damage Saddam, you'll see them pulling more behind us."
